title: Algorithmic trading enables emotionless, disciplined execution
claim: Algorithmic trading operates within parameters of cold logic and statistical probability, removing human emotional biases (fear, greed) that lead to suboptimal decisions and enabling disciplined adherence to trading plans

source.epub_locator: 1.2 Key Benefits of Algorithmic Trading: Mitigated Emotional Trading

mechanism: Systematic rule-based execution removes discretionary bias
assumptions: emotional discipline is necessary for trading profitability
validation: backtest performance vs manual trading; regime stability across market conditions

title: Portfolio theory foundation: efficient frontier optimizes risk-return tradeoff
claim: Markowitz portfolio theory (1952) posits that investors can optimize portfolio returns given a level of risk via diversification. The efficient frontier represents portfolios offering highest expected return for defined risk level or lowest risk for given return

source.epub_locator: 4.2 Portfolio Theory: Efficient Frontier and MPT

mechanism: Diversification reduces portfolio variance without proportional return reduction via correlation effects
validation: backtest portfolio optimization against buy-hold; test correlation stability in regimes

title: CAPM formula for expected return given risk-free rate, beta, market return
claim: Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) calculates expected return as: E[R] = r_f + beta * (r_m - r_f), where r_f is risk-free rate, beta is systematic risk, r_m is market return
mechanism: Linear relationship between systematic risk (beta) and expected return
assumptions: risk-free asset exists and rate is constant
validation: test beta calculation stability; compare CAPM expected vs realized returns; backtest portfolios weighted by CAPM

title: Backtesting framework must simulate real-world conditions including costs
claim: A backtesting framework is a simulation engine replicating historical market conditions. Credibility depends critically on fidelity to real market dynamics including liquidity, transaction costs, and temporal resolution of data

source.epub_locator: 6.2 Backtesting Frameworks: fidelity and market dynamics

mechanism: Unrealistic assumptions in backtest simulation lead to overoptimistic performance estimates and live failure
validation: compare backtest fill prices vs actual historical fills; sensitivity analysis on cost assumptions

title: Backtester should validate robustness across market conditions and time periods
claim: To ensure backtest credibility, strategies should be tested across multiple market regimes (trending, ranging, crisis), time periods, and synthetic perturbations (noise, liquidity shock) to detect overfitting and assess robustness
mechanism: Out-of-sample testing and stress testing reveal overfitting and identify failure modes
validation: walk-forward analysis; Monte Carlo perturbation; out-of-sample holdout validation

title: Strategy optimization bias: in-sample overfitting inflates backtest returns
claim: Strategies optimized on a fixed historical dataset often exhibit in-sample overfitting, showing high backtest returns that degrade significantly on out-of-sample data due to overfitting to noise rather than true signal
mechanism: Optimizer fits parameters to historical noise; generalizes poorly to new data
assumptions: optimization algorithm explores parameter space exhaustively
in-sample performance does not predict out-of-sample
failure_modes: false confidence from inflated backtest metrics
validation: compare in-sample vs out-of-sample Sharpe, max drawdown, win rate; holdout test set; Monte Carlo simulation of random optimization

title: High-frequency trading uses market-making and liquidity-provision strategies
claim: HFT algorithms employ market-making strategies, placing limit orders on both sides of the book, profiting from bid-ask spreads via inventory management. Characterized by high order-to-trade ratios, ultra-low latency, and high turnover
mechanism: Rapid quote updates and inventory rebalancing capture spread and manage directional risk
validation: backtest market-making in simulated orderbook; check inventory dynamics; compare vs live execution

title: Reinforcement learning for trading must model environment with states, actions, rewards
claim: Applying RL to trading requires careful design of environment (state space = market indicators + agent state, action space = buy/hold/sell, reward function = profit vs risk tradeoff) to learn optimal policies

source.epub_locator: 9.2 Reinforcement Learning for Trading: environment design

mechanism: RL agent learns via trial-and-error in simulated environment; reward function shapes learned behavior
validation: backtest RL policies; out-of-sample validation; check for reward gaming; live A/B test vs baseline

title: Direct Market Access (DMA) enables low-latency execution bypassing broker
claim: DMA is a trading system allowing direct interaction with exchange order book, bypassing broker, enabling traders to execute under own control with reduced latency and often reduced cost

source.section: 13.2 Direct Market Access (DMA) in Algorithmic Trading
source.epub_locator: 13.2 Direct Market Access: low-latency execution benefits

mechanism: Direct connection to exchange reduces order transmission latency; traders control entire execution pipeline
failure_modes: technology failure leads to uncontrolled trading
validation: verify DMA availability with intended brokers/exchanges; compare execution latency DMA vs broker

title: Order Management System (OMS) is core execution infrastructure component
claim: OMS is a trading system that manages orders, tracking order lifecycle from submission through fill, including order routing, risk checks, and compliance reporting

source.epub_locator: 13.1 Order Management Systems: order lifecycle and routing

mechanism: Centralized order management enables risk control, compliance, and audit trail
failure_modes: risk checks too loose causing over-trading
validation: test OMS order tracking accuracy; verify risk limits enforced; audit trail completeness

title: Transaction Cost Analysis (TCA) measures execution quality and market impact
claim: TCA quantifies trading costs including commissions, bid-ask spread, and market impact. Essential metric for assessing execution algorithm performance and strategy profitability
mechanism: TCA = (execution_price - decision_price) relative to market conditions = measure of slippage + market impact
validation: calculate TCA for sample orders; compare vs market benchmarks; track execution cost trends

title: Real-time market data feeds provide price, volume, order book depth
claim: Market data feeds supply price quotes, trade volumes, bid-ask spreads, and order book depth (pending orders at price levels). Granular market depth is essential for realistic backtesting and live execution

source.epub_locator: 14.2 Market Data Feeds: data granularity and order book

mechanism: Order book depth enables realistic slippage estimation and market impact modeling
assumptions: data feed is reliable and low-latency
validation: validate feed uptime and latency; check data integrity; test slippage estimation accuracy

title: Event-driven architecture enables reactive order processing in streaming context
claim: Event-driven systems react to market data events (ticks, fills, cancellations) to trigger order decisions and updates. Enables responsive real-time execution without polling
mechanism: Event-driven removes latency of polling; reduces resource contention
failure_modes: event ordering violation in asynchronous system
validation: test event ordering under load; measure event handler latency; simulate event loss and recovery

title: Real-time risk monitoring and alerting are essential safeguards
claim: Real-time risk assessment monitors positions, P&L, drawdowns, leverage, and concentration risk. Alerting system notifies traders of threshold breaches enabling rapid manual intervention
mechanism: Continuous monitoring + immediate alerting enables rapid response to adverse market moves
failure_modes: alert fatigue leading to ignored alerts
validation: test alert delivery latency; calibrate thresholds against live trading; test alert clarity

title: Value at Risk (VaR) quantifies portfolio loss at given confidence level
claim: VaR is a statistical measure of maximum portfolio loss within a time horizon at a given confidence level (e.g., 95% VaR = maximum loss with 95% probability). Used to set position limits and capital allocation

source.epub_locator: 4.3 Value at Risk: statistical risk measurement

mechanism: VaR captures tail risk; enables capital-efficient position sizing
validation: backtest VaR vs realized losses; stress test against tail scenarios; compare vs other risk metrics (CVaR)

title: Algorithmic trading regulations vary by jurisdiction (SEC, ESMA, FCA, IOSCO)
claim: Regulators including SEC (US), ESMA (EU), FCA (UK), and IOSCO (international) enforce algorithmic trading regulations emphasizing registration, pre/post-trade transparency, systems resilience, and prevention of market abuse

source.epub_locator: 15.2 Algorithmic Trading Regulations: SEC, ESMA, FCA, IOSCO

mechanism: Regulation imposes operational and compliance requirements; violations trigger fines or trading privileges revoked
validation: consult primary source regulatory documents (SEC Reg SHO, ESMA MIFID II, FCA Handbook); verify compliance framework with legal counsel

title: Compliance controls must prevent market abuse and ensure systems resilience
claim: Algorithmic trading systems must include pre-trade risk checks (position limits, leverage limits), post-trade compliance (transparency reporting), audit logging, business continuity planning, and circuit breakers to halt trading under extreme conditions

source.epub_locator: 15.3 Compliance and Controls: risk controls and audit trail

mechanism: Compliance controls prevent unintended market impact and enable regulatory audit
validation: test all pre-trade controls under stress; verify audit trail completeness; confirm business continuity procedures
